prerequisites: A probability distribution assigns mass to possible next tokens.
The target and draft models have different roles.
objective: Distinguish shared-context parallel marginals from autoregressive draft choices, then explain why a first target mismatch invalidates a later apparent match and commits the corrected greedy prefix.
scope: All twelve beats, including the repaired rejection example and target-only greedy comparison. This is not a stochastic distributional-equivalence demonstration or a benchmark.
assumptions: The draft marginals and target conditionals are invented, not measured.
Independent output choices mean factorization with shared conditioning fixed, not absence of shared target context.

Independently choose argmax from the real toy target conditionals and follow proposal-prefix membership. The last two target rows use rejected prefixes, so works and well are unused.

narration.text: A large language model generates tokens one at a time. Each new token requires a full forward pass through the target model. These empty slots represent the future tokens we need.

beats.purpose: A standard drafter fills successive slots.
beats.question: What does a normal drafter do?

narration.text: A standard draft model fills these slots one at a time, just like the target. It's faster per step, but still sequential. Each prediction waits for the previous one.

beats.purpose: All masked positions are predicted in one pass.
beats.question: How does DFlash do it differently?

narration.text: DFlash replaces this with parallel prediction. Instead of filling slots one by one, it masks the entire future block and predicts all positions in a single forward pass.

beats.purpose: Connect target hidden features to shared per-layer K/V draft context.
beats.question: Where does the draft model get its context?

narration.text: The key insight: DFlash borrows hidden features from the last target pass. These rich representations are projected and injected as keys and values into every layer of the small draft model.

beats.purpose: Reveal per-position distributions and label probabilities as toy values.
beats.question: What comes out of the draft pass?

narration.text: One draft pass produces a probability distribution for each masked position. These bars are toy probabilities, not measurements. Each column ranks possible tokens for its own position.

beats.purpose: Position two does not condition on the chosen position-one token.
beats.question: Why are these marginals, not conditionals?

narration.text: These marginals share the context, but not the chosen draft tokens. Position two doesn't condition on position one's choice. The drafter predicts all three before any within-block choice is made.

beats.purpose: Choose the modal toy path under an explicit temperature-zero regime.
beats.question: How do we pick tokens from these distributions?

narration.text: This example uses greedy decoding: temperature zero. Choose the largest probability in each column: 'the', 'model', 'works'. These are proposals, not yet committed output.

beats.purpose: Target the matches, then system disagrees with model at the first miss.
beats.question: How does the target verify these proposals?

narration.text: One causal target pass predicts next tokens along this draft path. 'The' matches. But the target chooses 'system', not 'model'. The accepted prefix stops before that first mismatch.

beats.purpose: Discard works despite agreement because its target row follows the rejected model prefix.
beats.question: Can a later matching token still be accepted?

narration.text: Even this later 'works' match cannot be kept. The target computed it after 'the model', not 'the system'. Discard the entire suffix from the mismatch onward.

beats.purpose: Commit the and target system; place bonus at the first miss, not after unused proposals.
beats.question: What happens to accepted and rejected tokens?

narration.text: Commit 'the', then the target's own 'system' at the first miss. This target token guarantees progress, even with zero draft matches. If every proposal matches, the bonus goes after the whole block.

beats.purpose: Separate target-only greedy equivalence from the progress guarantee.
beats.question: Why does this preserve target output semantics?

narration.text: Target-only greedy decoding also chooses 'the', then 'system'. Same target, same causal prefix, same tie-breaking: same greedy output. That is the correctness argument. The bonus guarantees progress, not a proof of distributional equivalence for sampling.

beats.purpose: Contrast one verified path with DDTree's retained alternatives.
beats.question: What if we could verify multiple paths at once?

narration.text: DFlash made the draft parallel, but we verified just one path. DDTree explores several likely continuations in one target pass. That's the next episode.

transfer_questions.question: The target row for works agrees with the third proposal. Why can't the final output append works after system?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: That row was computed after the model, not the corrected prefix the system. Only the is accepted before the first miss; emit system next and recompute from the corrected prefix.
transfer_questions.justification: The independently evaluated conditionals choose the at [], system at [the], and works at [the,model]. Membership stops at system because the proposal path only contains model there. The apparent later match has the wrong conditioning prefix.

transfer_questions.question: Does emitting at least one target token prove that any stochastic draft-acceptance rule is lossless?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: No. Progress and distributional correctness are different. This episode proves only the stated greedy-prefix argument; a stochastic rule needs its own target-distribution preservation argument.
transfer_questions.justification: The exact greedy target conditionals justify the accepted prefix and first-miss token here. A rule that always accepted arbitrary draft tokens could still append a target bonus while biasing earlier outputs, so the bonus cannot by itself prove equality of distributions.
